question: According to the manual, which of these trailer types is most likely to get stuck on a raised railroad-highway crossing because of low underneath clearance?
choice_a: A lowboy or possum-belly livestock trailer
choice_b: A flatbed trailer with tandem axles
choice_c: A standard enclosed dry van trailer
choice_d: A tanker trailer with extra ground clearance
explanation: The manual lists low slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers as being prone to getting stuck on raised railroad crossings due to low underneath clearance.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel vibrate
choice_b: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_c: Hearing the tires squeal
choice_d: Watching the speedometer drop suddenly
explanation: The manual states the earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is by seeing it in your mirrors, and to check them any time you apply the brakes hard.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What term describes the tendency of a vehicle's rear wheels to follow a different, tighter path than the front wheels when going around a corner?
choice_a: Off-tracking
choice_b: Drift correction
choice_c: Lateral sway
choice_d: Crack-the-whip effect
explanation: The manual explains that when a vehicle goes around a corner, the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels, and this is called off-tracking or "cheating."
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: Why should you never use the trailer hand valve to try to "straighten out" a skidding trailer?
choice_a: It drains the tractor's air tanks completely
choice_b: The trailer brakes caused the skid in the first place, so applying them again is the wrong thing to do
choice_c: It automatically sets the parking brake
choice_d: It disconnects the electrical cord to the trailer
explanation: The manual warns not to use the trailer hand brake to straighten out the rig because the brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: What is the only appropriate use of the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar) during normal operation?
choice_a: To test the trailer brakes
choice_b: As the primary brake while descending long grades
choice_c: To apply the brakes during normal driving
choice_d: To set the parking brake overnight
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes, and should not be used in driving because of the danger of making the trailer skid.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: While backing a trailer, if you see the trailer drifting off the proper path, what should you do?
choice_a: Immediately stop and pull all the way forward
choice_b: Correct it right away by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift
choice_c: Apply the trailer hand valve to stop the drift
choice_d: Wait until the drift becomes severe before correcting it
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to correct drift immediately: as soon as you see the trailer getting off the proper path, correct it by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: The tractor protection valve will close automatically when air pressure drops into approximately what range?
choice_a: 20 to 45 psi
choice_b: 5 to 15 psi
choice_c: 60 to 80 psi
choice_d: 100 to 120 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: On newer combination vehicles, what happens when you pull OUT the red eight-sided trailer air supply knob?
choice_a: It supplies air to the trailer brake system
choice_b: It shuts the air off and puts on the trailer emergency brakes
choice_c: It releases the tractor's parking brake
choice_d: It tests the antilock brake system
explanation: The manual explains you push the trailer air supply knob in to supply the trailer with air, and pull it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: When color-coded, what color is typically used to identify the service air-line versus the emergency (supply) air-line on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Blue for service, red for emergency
choice_b: Green for service, yellow for emergency
choice_c: Red for service, blue for emergency
choice_d: Black for service, white for emergency
explanation: The manual states that colors are sometimes used to avoid mistakes when coupling glad hands: blue is used for the service lines and red for the emergency (supply) lines.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: What is the danger of connecting a tractor's air-lines to a trailer in the wrong (crossed) configuration?
choice_a: The trailer brake lights will stop working
choice_b: Supply air goes to the service line instead of charging the trailer tanks, so air is not available to release the trailer spring brakes and you could end up with no trailer brakes
choice_c: The tractor's engine will not start
choice_d: The turn signals will flash out of sync
explanation: The manual warns that if you cross the air-lines, supply air will be sent to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so air will not be available to release the trailer spring brakes — a very dangerous situation.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: On a combination pulling a single trailer that is not itself towing another trailer, what position should the shut-off valves at the very back of that last trailer be in?
choice_a: Open
choice_b: Closed
choice_c: Set to the "emergency" position
choice_d: Removed entirely from the air-lines
explanation: The manual states that all shut-off valves must be in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: Why is it especially important to use wheel chocks when parking a trailer that does not have spring brakes?
choice_a: The emergency brakes only hold as long as air pressure remains in the trailer tank, and that air will eventually leak away, leaving no brakes
choice_b: Chocks are just a required backup even though spring brakes hold indefinitely
choice_c: Chocks are required by law regardless of the brake type installed
choice_d: Chocks prevent the landing gear from collapsing under load
explanation: The manual explains that on trailers without spring brakes, the emergency brakes hold only as long as there is air pressure in the trailer air tank; eventually the air leaks away and there will be no brakes, so it is very important to use wheel chocks.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to be equipped with antilock brake systems (ABS)?
choice_a: January 1, 1990
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: September 1, 2000
choice_d: July 1, 2005
explanation: The manual states that all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: According to the manual, does having ABS necessarily shorten a combination vehicle's stopping distance?
choice_a: Yes, ABS always significantly shortens stopping distance
choice_b: No, ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_c: Only when the road is wet
choice_d: Only when both the tractor and trailer are equipped with ABS
explanation: The manual explicitly states that ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: When positioning the tractor to couple with a semitrailer, why should you never back under the trailer at an angle?
choice_a: It could damage the fifth wheel grease fitting
choice_b: You might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_c: It could trigger the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_d: It could cross the service and emergency air-lines
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to put the tractor directly in front of the trailer and never back under it at an angle, because doing so might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: When checking trailer height before coupling, what problem can occur if the trailer is set too low?
choice_a: The tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose
choice_b: The kingpin will not fit into the fifth wheel at all
choice_c: The landing gear will refuse to lower
choice_d: The air-lines will automatically disconnect
explanation: The manual states that if the trailer is too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose; if the trailer is too high, it may not couple correctly.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: After backing the tractor under the trailer during coupling, how do you check that the fifth wheel has locked securely onto the kingpin?
choice_a: Listen for a single clicking sound and assume it is locked
choice_b: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked
choice_c: Immediately drive at highway speed to test the connection
choice_d: Disconnect the air-lines and see whether the trailer rolls
explanation: In the "Check Connection for Security" step, the manual instructs raising the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pulling the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-8

question: Why should you never drive with the trailer landing gear only partway raised?
choice_a: It increases fuel consumption
choice_b: It may catch on railroad tracks or other things
choice_c: It automatically disconnects the emergency air-line
choice_d: It causes the ABS malfunction lamp to illuminate
explanation: The manual warns to never drive with the landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-8

question: When unlocking the fifth wheel during uncoupling, what safety precaution does the manual specify regarding your body position?
choice_a: Keep legs and feet clear of the rear tractor wheels to avoid serious injury if the vehicle moves
choice_b: Stand directly behind the trailer wheels for a clear view
choice_c: Kneel under the fifth wheel to watch it release
choice_d: Place one foot on the tractor frame for balance
explanation: In the "Unlock Fifth Wheel" step, the manual instructs keeping legs and feet clear of the rear tractor wheels to avoid serious injury in case the vehicle moves.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-9

question: When pulling the tractor forward to clear the fifth wheel during uncoupling, why does the manual say to stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer rather than pulling all the way clear right away?
choice_a: To keep the parking brake engaged longer
choice_b: This prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink
choice_c: To allow the electrical cord to be reconnected first
choice_d: To make it easier to re-couple to the same trailer immediately
explanation: The manual instructs pulling the tractor forward until the fifth wheel comes out from under the trailer, but stopping with the tractor frame under the trailer, which prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-9

question: According to the manual's warning, what can happen if the pintle hook latch is not correctly locked?
choice_a: Only a minor rattling noise while driving
choice_b: Separation of the trailer and vehicle, which if not avoided could result in death or serious injury
choice_c: A slight decrease in fuel economy
choice_d: Flickering of the trailer running lights
explanation: The manual states that failure to correctly lock the latch can result in separation of the trailer and vehicle, which, if not avoided, could result in death or serious injury.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-10

question: What is the first step listed for uncoupling a pintle hook trailer?
choice_a: Rotate the jack handle to extend the jack
choice_b: Park the trailer on a firm, level surface and block the trailer tires
choice_c: Disconnect the safety chains from the tow vehicle
choice_d: Unlock the coupler and open it
explanation: Step 1 of Uncoupling a Pintle Hook is to park the trailer on a firm level surface and block the trailer tires.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-10

question: According to the manual, what is required by law on all trailers, and must be attached when coupling a gooseneck hitch?
choice_a: A rearview backup camera
choice_b: Safety chains
choice_c: A spare tire
choice_d: A supplemental trailer brake controller
explanation: The manual instructs attaching safety chains when coupling a gooseneck hitch and notes that all trailers are required by law to have safety chains.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-11

question: What is the very first step when uncoupling a drawbar-type trailer?
choice_a: Remove the rubber dust-proof bellows protection cover
choice_b: Make sure that the trailer brake is on
choice_c: Loosen the adjustment screw
choice_d: Remove the safety lock screw and self-locking nut
explanation: The manual's uncoupling-a-drawbar procedure begins with Step 1, Turn Trailer Brake On: make sure that the trailer brake is on.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-11

question: When inspecting the lower fifth wheel, the locking jaws should be closed around what part of the kingpin rather than the head?
choice_a: The shank
choice_b: The base plate
choice_c: The grease fitting
choice_d: The safety latch handle
explanation: The manual's coupling-system inspection checklist specifies checking that the locking jaws are around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-12

question: During the walk-around inspection of a combination vehicle, what should you verify about the landing gear?
choice_a: It is fully raised, with no missing parts, and not bent or otherwise damaged, with the crank handle in place and secured
choice_b: It has been repainted within the last year
choice_c: It is disconnected from the trailer frame for storage
choice_d: It has a functioning horn attached
explanation: The manual's inspection checklist for the landing gear specifies that it should be fully raised, with no missing parts, not bent or otherwise damaged, and that the crank handle be in place and secured.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-12

question: When testing that air flows all the way to the back of a combination vehicle, what should you do at the rear of the last trailer to confirm the system is charged?
choice_a: Open the emergency line shut-off valve and listen for air escaping
choice_b: Disconnect the electrical cord and check for sparking
choice_c: Remove the wheel chocks and let the trailer roll
choice_d: Apply the parking brake and rev the engine
explanation: The manual's brake-check procedure has you open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; you should hear air escaping, showing the entire system is charged.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-13

question: How do you test that the trailer service brakes are connected and working, using the hand control (trolley valve)?
choice_a: Push the trailer air supply knob in and out repeatedly while parked
choice_b: Move the vehicle forward slowly and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control; you should feel the brakes come on
choice_c: Disconnect the emergency line and watch for a pressure drop on the gauge
choice_d: Rev the engine while the vehicle is stationary and listen for air leaks
explanation: The manual's Test Trailer Service Brakes procedure has you move the vehicle forward slowly and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control (trolley valve); feeling the brakes come on tells you the trailer brakes are connected and working.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-13

question: In a combination pulling more than one trailer, which unit's rear wheels off-track the most when turning a corner?
choice_a: The rear wheels of the powered unit (truck or tractor)
choice_b: The rear wheels of the last trailer
choice_c: The rear wheels of the first trailer only
choice_d: All units off-track by exactly the same amount
explanation: The manual states that the rear wheels of the powered unit off-track some, the rear wheels of the trailer off-track even more, and if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer off-track the most.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: When you must back a trailer along a curved path, which side should you back toward, and why?
choice_a: The passenger's side, because it gives a wider view of the curb
choice_b: The driver's side, so you can see
choice_c: Whichever side has more traffic, for visibility to other drivers
choice_d: It does not matter as long as you use a spotter
explanation: The manual advises that whenever you back up with a trailer, try to position your vehicle so you can back in a straight line, and if you must back on a curved path, back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2
